title: Exploring the Story World of Pompeii
lesson_overview: Pupils are introduced to 'Escape from Pompeii' through a shared read-aloud, exploring the setting, characters and overall story arc. They discuss their initial responses and begin to identify the main events.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify the main characters, setting and key events in 'Escape from Pompeii'.
success_criteria: I can name the main characters in the story.
I can describe the setting of Pompeii using evidence from the text and illustrations.
I can identify at least three key events from the story.
main_activity: The teacher reads the whole book aloud, pausing to discuss the illustrations and key moments. Pupils then work in pairs to complete a 'story snapshot' sheet where they record the main characters, the setting and three events they remember. Pairs share back with the class to build a whole-class list of key events on the board.
teacher_notes: Display a map of Roman Italy and an image of Vesuvius to build geographical context before reading — this supports pupil engagement and comprehension of the setting.

nc_links.curriculumLink: English KS2 — Spoken language: listen and respond appropriately to adults and their peers
English KS2 — Reading/Comprehension: identifying themes and conventions in a wide range of books
English KS2 — Reading/Comprehension: discussing books, poems and other works that are read to them and those they can read for themselves

eal: Pair EAL pupils with a supportive talk partner and pre-teach key vocabulary such as 'volcano', 'eruption', 'harbour' and 'escape' using illustrated flashcards before the read-aloud.
lower: Provide a pre-prepared list of character names and a word bank of setting vocabulary to support the story snapshot activity.
Use a simple three-box template labelled 'Beginning', 'Middle' and 'End' to help pupils organise their thoughts.
higher: Ask pupils to consider why the author chose to set the story in Pompeii and what effect this has on the reader.
Challenge pupils to begin ordering the events they identified into a rough timeline independently.

title: Sequencing the Story
lesson_overview: Pupils revisit the text to identify and sequence the key events in the correct order. They discuss how the story is structured, including the build-up, climax and resolution, and begin to understand narrative shape.
learning_intention: We are learning to sequence the key events of the story and understand how the narrative is structured.
success_criteria: I can put the key events of the story into the correct order.
I can identify the build-up, climax and resolution in the story.
I can explain why the order of events is important to the story.
main_activity: The teacher models identifying the narrative structure using a simple story mountain visual. Pupils are given a set of illustrated event cards showing key moments from the story and work in small groups to sequence them correctly, justifying their choices. Groups compare their sequences and discuss any differences using the book as a reference.
teacher_notes: Prepare a set of eight to ten illustrated event cards in advance — including images as well as short captions supports all learners in accessing the sequencing task.

nc_links.curriculumLink: English KS2 — Reading/Comprehension: summarise the main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph, identifying key details that support the main ideas
English KS2 — Reading/Comprehension: identifying how language, structure and presentation contribute to meaning
English KS2 — Spoken language: participate in discussions, presentations, performances, role play, improvisations and debates

eal: Ensure event cards include both images and simple sentences. Allow EAL pupils to discuss the sequence in their home language with a bilingual partner before feeding back in English.
lower: Reduce the number of event cards to five or six and include clear illustrated images on each card to support recognition.
Provide a partially completed story mountain with some events already placed to scaffold the sequencing.
higher: Ask pupils to write a one-sentence caption for each event card in their own words, focusing on precise vocabulary.
Challenge pupils to identify turning points in the story and explain how the author builds tension.

title: Creating an Illustrated Story Map
lesson_overview: The teacher models how to create an illustrated story map, demonstrating how to represent key events as labelled pictures arranged in sequence. Pupils then begin creating their own story maps using their sequenced event cards as a guide.
learning_intention: We are learning to create an illustrated story map that shows the key events of the story in sequence.
success_criteria: I can plan my story map by selecting the most important events to include.
I can draw and label each key event clearly on my story map.
I can arrange my events in the correct order on my map.
main_activity: The teacher uses a visualiser or large paper to model creating a story map, thinking aloud about which events to include and how to represent them visually with a label or short caption. Pupils then create their own A3 story maps, drawing and labelling between six and eight key events in sequence. They are encouraged to use vocabulary from the book in their labels.
teacher_notes: Display a completed model story map on the working wall throughout the unit so pupils can refer to it as a scaffold when creating their own and when retelling.

nc_links.curriculumLink: English KS2 — Writing/Planning: discussing and recording ideas
English KS2 — Writing/Vocabulary, grammar and punctuation: extending the range of sentences with more than one clause by using a wider range of conjunctions
English KS2 — Writing/Handwriting: increasing the legibility, consistency and quality of their handwriting

eal: Provide a vocabulary mat with key words and phrases from the story illustrated with pictures to support caption writing.
lower: Provide a pre-drawn story map template with boxes for pupils to illustrate and simple sentence starters for the captions.
Allow pupils to use their sequenced event cards directly as a reference while creating their map.
higher: Encourage pupils to include additional detail in their captions, such as character feelings or the author's descriptive language.
Ask pupils to annotate their map with notes about how the mood or atmosphere changes across the story.

title: Oral Retelling Using Story Maps
lesson_overview: Pupils use their completed story maps to practise retelling the story orally, focusing on sequencing language, expressive voice and key details. They rehearse with a partner before performing to a small group.
learning_intention: We are learning to retell the story orally in sequence using our story maps as a guide.
success_criteria: I can use my story map to retell the key events in the correct order.
I can use time connectives and sequencing language when I retell the story.
I can include detail about characters and setting in my retelling.
main_activity: The teacher models an oral retelling using the class story map, demonstrating the use of time connectives such as 'first', 'then', 'suddenly' and 'finally'. Pupils practise their own retelling with a talk partner, using their story maps as prompts and giving each other feedback on sequence and detail. Selected pupils then perform their retelling to a small group or the class.
teacher_notes: Create a 'storytelling toolkit' display or bookmark with useful time connectives and descriptive phrases from the book to support pupils during oral retelling.

nc_links.curriculumLink: English KS2 — Spoken language: give well-structured descriptions, explanations and narratives for different purposes, including for expressing feelings
English KS2 — Writing/Vocabulary, grammar and punctuation: using conjunctions, adverbs and prepositions to express time, place and cause
English KS2 — Spoken language: maintain attention and participate actively in collaborative conversations, staying on topic and initiating and responding to comments

eal: Allow EAL pupils to rehearse their retelling multiple times with the same supportive partner before performing to a group, building confidence through repetition.
lower: Allow pupils to point to each image on their story map as they retell, reducing the verbal memory load.
Provide a sentence frame strip such as 'First… Next… Then… Suddenly… Finally…' for pupils to follow during their retelling.
higher: Challenge pupils to retell without looking at their story map for at least part of the story, relying on memory.
Encourage pupils to vary their tone of voice and pace to build tension at the climax of the story.

title: Writing a Story Retelling
lesson_overview: Building on their oral retellings, pupils plan and write a structured written retelling of the story using their story maps as a framework. The teacher models writing the opening and supports pupils in developing their use of descriptive language and connectives.
learning_intention: We are learning to write a retelling of the story in sequence using descriptive language and time connectives.
success_criteria: I can use my story map to write the key events in the correct order.
I can use time connectives to link events in my writing.
I can include descriptive details about the characters and setting.
main_activity: The teacher models writing the opening paragraph of the retelling using a shared writing approach, thinking aloud about word choices and the use of time connectives. Pupils then write their own retelling independently, using their story maps as a guide and referring to the storytelling toolkit for vocabulary support. Pupils aim to write a paragraph for each key section of the story map.
teacher_notes: Encourage pupils to re-read their writing after each paragraph to check it makes sense and flows — a simple 'read it back' routine supports self-editing and improves writing quality.

nc_links.curriculumLink: English KS2 — Writing/Composition: writing narratives about personal experiences and those of others (real and fictional)
English KS2 — Writing/Vocabulary, grammar and punctuation: using conjunctions, adverbs and prepositions to express time, place and cause
English KS2 — Writing/Composition: organising paragraphs around a theme

eal: Provide a bilingual word mat and allow EAL pupils to draft key sentences in their first language before translating, supporting idea generation before the challenge of writing in English.
lower: Provide a writing frame with paragraph starters and a word bank of key vocabulary and time connectives.
Allow pupils to dictate one or two sections to a teaching assistant who scribes before the pupil continues independently.
higher: Challenge pupils to include dialogue between characters and use a range of sentence types to vary the pace of their writing.
Encourage the use of powerful vocabulary drawn directly from the original text, with pupils explaining why the author chose those words.

title: Sharing and Celebrating Our Retellings
lesson_overview: Pupils complete and edit their written retellings, then share their story maps and writing with an audience. The lesson celebrates their learning across the unit and consolidates their understanding of narrative structure.
learning_intention: We are learning to edit our writing for clarity and share our story retelling with an audience.
success_criteria: I can re-read my writing and make improvements to vocabulary and punctuation.
I can present my story map and retelling clearly to an audience.
I can explain how my story map helped me to plan and retell the story.
main_activity: Pupils spend time editing and improving their written retellings using a simple editing checklist focusing on punctuation, time connectives and descriptive language. They then display their illustrated story maps alongside their writing for a gallery walk, where classmates use sticky notes to leave positive feedback. Selected pupils share their oral or written retelling with the class as a celebration of their work.
teacher_notes: Consider inviting another class or parents to the gallery walk to give pupils a genuine and motivating audience for their completed story maps and retellings.

nc_links.curriculumLink: English KS2 — Writing/Composition: assessing the effectiveness of their own and others' writing and suggesting improvements
English KS2 — Spoken language: perform their own compositions, using appropriate intonation, volume and movement so that meaning is clear
English KS2 — Writing/Composition: proof-read for spelling and punctuation errors

eal: Allow EAL pupils to present their story map orally rather than in writing if appropriate, celebrating their oral retelling as a valid final outcome.
lower: Provide a simplified editing checklist with two or three focused targets, such as checking capital letters and adding a time connective to each paragraph.
Sit lower attaining pupils with a teaching assistant during the editing phase to support identification of improvements.
higher: Ask pupils to write a brief author's note explaining the choices they made in their retelling, such as vocabulary decisions or structural choices.
Challenge pupils to peer-edit a partner's work, providing specific written feedback using the success criteria as a guide.
